rows.stem: Which of the following molecules has a chiral centre correctly labelled with an asterisk (*) ?
rows.solution:
The asterisk is correctly placed in \(\mathrm{CH_3C^{*}HClCH_2Br}\).

A CHIRAL CENTRE is a carbon carrying FOUR DIFFERENT groups. Check the marked carbon in each.

In the answer the marked carbon holds \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\), \(-\mathrm{H}\), \(-\mathrm{Cl}\) and \(-\mathrm{CH_2Br}\) — four different groups, so it is genuinely chiral.

In \(\mathrm{CH_3C^{*}HBrCH_3}\) the marked carbon holds TWO METHYL groups, which are identical. In \(\mathrm{CH_3C^{*}Br_2CH_3}\) it holds two methyls AND two bromines — worse on both counts.

The third structure is the subtle one. Its marked carbon holds \(-\mathrm{H}\), \(-\mathrm{OH}\) and TWO \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) groups, and those two are identical, so it is not chiral either. This is glycerol, which is achiral despite looking promising.

The test is always the same: compare the four attached groups as WHOLE groups, not just the atoms directly bonded.

rows.stem: Which of the following alcohols will not undergo oxidation ?
rows.solution:
2-METHYLBUTAN-2-OL will not undergo oxidation.

Oxidising an alcohol requires removing a hydrogen from the carbon bearing the hydroxyl, so that carbon must HAVE one. A TERTIARY alcohol has none — its carbinol carbon is bonded to three carbons and the hydroxyl, with no hydrogen left.

Classify the four. Butanol is PRIMARY, and oxidises to butanal and then butanoic acid. Butan-2-ol and 3-methylbutan-2-ol are both SECONDARY, each having one hydrogen on the carbinol carbon, and both oxidise to ketones.

In 2-methylbutan-2-ol the hydroxyl sits on a carbon carrying a methyl, an ethyl and another methyl — three carbons, no hydrogen — so it is TERTIARY and resists oxidation under ordinary conditions.

It CAN be oxidised under drastic conditions with a strong oxidising agent, but only by breaking carbon-carbon bonds and shattering the molecule, which is a different process altogether.

rows.stem:
A voltaic cell is made by connecting two half cells represented by half equations below :
\(\mathrm{Sn^{2+}_{(aq)}} + 2\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Sn_{(s)}}\)  \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ} = -\,0.14\) V
\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}_{(aq)}} + \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe^{2+}_{(aq)}}\)  \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ} = +\,0.77\) V
Which statement is correct about this voltaic cell ?

options.label: A
options.text: \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is oxidised and the voltage of the cell is \(-0.91\) V

options.label: B
options.text: Sn is oxidised and the voltage of the cell is \(0.91\) V

options.label: C
options.text: \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is oxidised and the voltage of the cell is \(0.91\) V

options.label: D
options.text: Sn is oxidised and the voltage of the cell is \(0.63\) V

rows.solution:
Tin is oxidised and the cell voltage is \(0{\cdot}91\) V.

The half cell with the HIGHER reduction potential acts as the CATHODE, since it has the stronger pull on electrons. Here that is the iron couple at \(+0{\cdot}77\) V, so iron(III) is reduced to iron(II) and the tin half cell must be the ANODE — tin metal is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Sn^{2+}}\).

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = 0{\cdot}77 - (-0{\cdot}14) = 0{\cdot}91\ \mathrm{V}\)

Two checks dispose of the other options. A VOLTAIC cell runs spontaneously, so its emf must be POSITIVE — that removes the negative value at once. And it is iron(III) that is REDUCED, not iron(II) oxidised, which removes both options naming \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) as the species oxidised.

Note also that the potentials are NOT multiplied by the number of electrons before subtracting. Electrode potential is an intensive property, so balancing the electrons does not change either value.

rows.stem:
Four half reactions I to IV are shown below :
I.  \(2\mathrm{Cl^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl_2} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}}\)
II.  \(4\mathrm{OH^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{O_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}}\)
III.  \(\mathrm{Na^{+}} + \mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}\)
IV.  \(2\mathrm{H^{+}} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_2}\)
Which two of these reactions are most likely to occur when concentrated brine is electrolysed ?
rows.solution:
The two reactions are chlorine evolution at the anode and hydrogen evolution at the cathode.

At the CATHODE the candidates are sodium ion and hydrogen ion. Water is far more easily reduced than \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) — sodium's reduction potential is \(-2{\cdot}71\) V against hydrogen's \(0{\cdot}00\) V — so HYDROGEN is liberated and sodium remains in solution. Sodium metal can only be obtained from the MOLTEN salt, where no water is present.

At the ANODE the candidates are chloride and hydroxide. On the standard potentials alone oxygen should win, needing \(+1{\cdot}23\) V against chlorine's \(+1{\cdot}36\) V — but it does not, because liberating oxygen requires a large OVERPOTENTIAL and chlorine almost none. With CONCENTRATED brine the chloride concentration tips the balance further, and CHLORINE is evolved.

This pair of reactions is the industrial CHLOR-ALKALI process, which supplies chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide from brine.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which property of transition metals enables them to behave as catalysts ?
rows.solution:
VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES enable transition metals to act as catalysts.

A catalyst works by offering a path of LOWER ACTIVATION ENERGY, and a transition metal does so by forming an INTERMEDIATE with the reactants — accepting electrons from one and passing them to another, then returning to its original state so that it is not consumed.

That electron shuttling requires the metal to move easily between oxidation states, which is exactly what a partly filled d subshell allows. Vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process is the standard illustration, cycling between \(+5\) and \(+4\) as it oxidises sulphur dioxide.

The other properties are real but not the reason. A high melting point, alloy formation and a high ionisation enthalpy all follow from the same d electrons, yet none of them provides a route for the reaction.

Transition metals also catalyse by ADSORPTION on a finely divided surface, as iron does in the Haber process — but even there the surface bonding involves the d orbitals.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem: In the two tetrahedral structures of dichromate ion

options.label: A
options.text: 4 Cr – O bonds are equivalent in length.

options.label: B
options.text: 6 Cr – O bonds are equivalent in length.

options.label: C
options.text: All Cr – O bonds are equivalent in length.

options.label: D
options.text: All Cr – O bonds are non-equivalent.

rows.solution:
SIX of the chromium-oxygen bonds are equivalent in length.

The dichromate ion is two \(\mathrm{CrO_4}\) tetrahedra joined at a CORNER, sharing ONE oxygen atom between them. That gives eight oxygens in all: six TERMINAL, three on each chromium, and one BRIDGING.

The six terminal bonds are all alike, each about 163 pm, and short because of \(\pi\) bonding between the oxygen and the metal.

The two bonds to the BRIDGING oxygen are different — longer, about 179 pm — because that oxygen must share itself between two chromium atoms and cannot form the same \(\pi\) bond to either.

So the bonds fall into two sets of six and two, and neither "all equivalent" nor "all non-equivalent" describes the ion. The chromate ion by contrast, having no bridge, does have all four of its bonds equivalent.

rows.stem: 1 mole of liquid A and 2 moles of liquid B make a solution having a total vapour pressure 40 torr. The vapour pressure of pure A and pure B are 45 torr and 30 torr respectively. The above solution
rows.solution:
The solution shows POSITIVE DEVIATION from Raoult's law.

Find what Raoult's law predicts, then compare. The mole fractions are \(x_A = \frac{1}{3}\) and \(x_B = \frac{2}{3}\):
\(p_{\text{ideal}} = x_A p_A^{\circ} + x_B p_B^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{3}(45) + \dfrac{2}{3}(30)\)
\(= 15 + 20 = 35\ \text{torr}\)

The OBSERVED total pressure is 40 torr, which is HIGHER than the predicted 35 — and a vapour pressure above the ideal value is a positive deviation by definition.

The molecular meaning: the attraction between UNLIKE molecules is WEAKER than that between like ones, so the molecules escape the liquid more readily than they would from their own kind.

The accompanying signs all follow. Mixing is ENDOTHERMIC and the mixture cools, the volume INCREASES, and if an azeotrope forms it is a MINIMUM boiling one — so the last option is wrong on both counts.

rows.stem: Which of the following would not be a good choice for reducing nitrobenzene to aniline ?
rows.solution:
LITHIUM ALUMINIUM HYDRIDE would be the poor choice.

Reducing a nitro group to an amino group requires SIX hydrogen atoms, the nitrogen falling from \(+3\) to \(-3\). Three of the options do it cleanly: hydrogen over nickel, iron with hydrochloric acid, and tin with hydrochloric acid — the last two supplying nascent hydrogen in the reaction mixture.

Lithium aluminium hydride is a HYDRIDE donor, delivering \(\mathrm{H^-}\) to an electrophilic centre. It excels at carbonyl compounds, nitriles and amides. With a nitro group it does not reduce cleanly through to the amine, giving instead AZO and other partially reduced products.

There is also a practical objection. Iron with hydrochloric acid is cheap and the iron(II) chloride formed is harmless; lithium aluminium hydride is expensive, reacts violently with water and demands strictly dry ether.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: If molality of a dilute solution is doubled, the value of the molal elevation constant \((\mathrm{K_b})\) will be
rows.solution:
The molal elevation constant is UNCHANGED.

\(\mathrm{K_b}\) is a property of the SOLVENT ALONE. It does not depend on what is dissolved in it, nor on how much:
\(\Delta \mathrm{T_b} = \mathrm{K_b}\,m\)

What doubles when the molality doubles is the ELEVATION \(\Delta \mathrm{T_b}\), not the constant that connects the two. Confusing the two is exactly what the question tests.

Its meaning is definite: \(\mathrm{K_b}\) is the elevation in boiling point a 1 molal solution would produce, and for water it is \(0{\cdot}512\) K kg per mole whatever the solute. It can be calculated from the solvent's boiling point and its enthalpy of vaporisation, quantities in which no solute appears:
\(\mathrm{K_b} = \dfrac{\mathrm{R}\,\mathrm{T_b}^2\,\mathrm{M_1}}{1000\,\Delta_{\text{vap}}\mathrm{H}}\)

The same holds for \(\mathrm{K_f}\), the molal depression constant.

rows.stem: Hydrolysis of sucrose is called
rows.solution:
The hydrolysis of sucrose is called INVERSION.

The name records a change of OPTICAL ROTATION. Sucrose is DEXTROROTATORY, with a specific rotation of \(+66{\cdot}5^{\circ}\). On hydrolysis it gives equal amounts of glucose and fructose:
glucose, \(+52{\cdot}5^{\circ}\); fructose, \(-92{\cdot}4^{\circ}\)

Fructose rotates to the LEFT more strongly than glucose rotates to the right, so the mixture comes out LAEVOROTATORY at about \(-20^{\circ}\) — the sign has INVERTED, from plus to minus.

The product mixture is therefore called INVERT SUGAR, and it is what honey largely consists of.

The other terms belong elsewhere: hydration adds water across a bond without breaking the molecule, esterification joins an acid and an alcohol, and saponification hydrolyses a fat with alkali to give soap.

rows.stem: Which one of the following has lowest \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) value ?
rows.solution:
NITROACETIC ACID, \(\mathrm{O_2N{-}CH_2{-}COOH}\), has the lowest \(\mathrm{pK_a}\).

Read the scale first. A LOWER \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) means a STRONGER acid, so the question asks which acid is strongest — and that is decided by how stable the carboxylate ion left behind is.

Anything that WITHDRAWS electron density spreads the negative charge and stabilises the anion. The NITRO group is the most powerful withdrawer here, pulling both inductively and by resonance onto its own two oxygens; chlorine withdraws inductively only, and less strongly.

The measured values confirm the order: nitroacetic acid 1.68, chloroacetic acid 2.86, formic acid 3.75, acetic acid 4.76.

Acetic acid is the WEAKEST because its methyl group RELEASES density, intensifying the charge on the anion. Formic acid, having only a hydrogen in that position, has no such disadvantage and is stronger than acetic — which is the smaller comparison hidden inside the question.

rows.stem: Which of the following cell was used in Apollo space programme ?
rows.solution:
The HYDROGEN-OXYGEN FUEL CELL was used in the Apollo space programme.

A fuel cell converts the energy of COMBUSTION of a fuel DIRECTLY into electrical energy, with the reactants supplied continuously from outside rather than stored inside. Hydrogen is oxidised at one porous carbon electrode, oxygen reduced at the other, with aqueous potassium hydroxide between them:
\(2\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Three features suited it to a spacecraft. It is EFFICIENT, around 70%, since the energy never passes through heat and is not limited by the Carnot efficiency. It is POLLUTION FREE. And its only product is WATER — which the crew drank.

The other cells could not have served. The Daniell cell and dry cell are heavy and exhaust themselves; the mercury cell gives a very steady but tiny current, suited to a watch rather than a spacecraft.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The following experimental rate data were obtained for a reaction carried out at 25 °C :
\(\mathrm{A_{(g)}} + \mathrm{B_{(g)}} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_{(g)}} + \mathrm{D_{(g)}}\)

| Initial \([\mathrm{A_{(g)}}]\)/mol \(\mathrm{dm^{-3}}\) | Initial \([\mathrm{B_{(g)}}]\)/mol \(\mathrm{dm^{-3}}\) | Initial rate/mol \(\mathrm{dm^{-3}s^{-1}}\) |
|---|---|---|
| \(3.0 \times 10^{-2}\) | \(2.0 \times 10^{-2}\) | \(1.89 \times 10^{-4}\) |
| \(3.0 \times 10^{-2}\) | \(4.0 \times 10^{-2}\) | \(1.89 \times 10^{-4}\) |
| \(6.0 \times 10^{-2}\) | \(4.0 \times 10^{-2}\) | \(7.56 \times 10^{-4}\) |

What are the orders with respect to \(\mathrm{A_{(g)}}\) and \(\mathrm{B_{(g)}}\) ?

options.label: A
options.text: Order with respect to \(\mathrm{A_{(g)}}\) : Zero; Order with respect to \(\mathrm{B_{(g)}}\) : Second

options.label: B
options.text: Order with respect to \(\mathrm{A_{(g)}}\) : First; Order with respect to \(\mathrm{B_{(g)}}\) : Zero

options.label: C
options.text: Order with respect to \(\mathrm{A_{(g)}}\) : Second; Order with respect to \(\mathrm{B_{(g)}}\) : Zero

options.label: D
options.text: Order with respect to \(\mathrm{A_{(g)}}\) : Second; Order with respect to \(\mathrm{B_{(g)}}\) : First

rows.solution:
The order is SECOND in A and ZERO in B.

Compare experiments in which only one concentration changes.

ORDER IN B — the first two experiments have \([\mathrm{A}]\) fixed at \(3{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-2}\). Doubling \([\mathrm{B}]\) leaves the rate at \(1{\cdot}89 \times 10^{-4}\), exactly UNCHANGED. A concentration that does not affect the rate enters to the power ZERO.

ORDER IN A — the second and third experiments have \([\mathrm{B}]\) fixed at \(4{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-2}\). Doubling \([\mathrm{A}]\) raises the rate from \(1{\cdot}89 \times 10^{-4}\) to \(7{\cdot}56 \times 10^{-4}\), a factor of FOUR:
\(2^{\,p} = 4\), so \(p = 2\)

The rate law is \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^2\) and the overall order is 2.

A zero order in B does not mean B takes no part — it must, since it appears in the equation. It means B is not involved up to and including the SLOW step of the mechanism, which is what makes order an experimental result rather than something read off the equation.

rows.stem:
The magnetic moment of \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\)
[Atomic number : Ni = 28]
rows.solution:
The magnetic moment is about \(2{\cdot}82\) B.M.

Nickel is atomic number 28, so the atom is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^8 4s^2\). Four chlorides give \(-4\) against an overall \(-2\), so nickel is \(+2\) and \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\).

CHLORIDE is a WEAK FIELD ligand. It does not force the electrons to pair, so the eight d electrons spread out as far as Hund's rule allows — three pairs and TWO UNPAIRED electrons.

Substituting into the spin-only formula with \(n = 2\):
\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{2 \times 4} = \sqrt{8}\)

\(\mu = 2{\cdot}83\) B.M.

The other values correspond to other electron counts, and each can be recognised: 1.73 for one unpaired electron, 3.87 for three, 4.90 for four, 5.92 for five. Learning that short list makes such questions a matter of counting rather than of arithmetic.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Proteins are polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids connected by a peptide bond.
Reason (R) : A tetrapeptide contains 4 amino acids linked by 4 peptide bonds.
rows.context: For questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Proteins ARE polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids joined by peptide bonds — the Assertion is correct, and "\(\alpha\)" matters, meaning the amino group sits on the carbon next to the carboxyl.

The Reason gets the ARITHMETIC wrong. A tetrapeptide has four amino acids but only THREE peptide bonds, not four — each bond joins a neighbouring PAIR, and four units in a chain have three junctions between them.

The general rule is that a peptide of \(n\) residues contains \(n - 1\) peptide bonds, and \(n - 1\) molecules of water are lost in building it.

Four bonds would require the chain to close into a RING, which is what a cyclic peptide does — but an ordinary tetrapeptide is open, with a free amino group at one end and a free carboxyl at the other.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : For a zero order reaction the unit of rate constant and rate of reaction are same.
Reason (R) : Rate of reaction for zero order reaction is independent of concentration of reactant.
rows.context: For questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.

For a reaction of order \(n\), rearranging the rate law gives
\(k = \dfrac{\text{Rate}}{[\mathrm{A}]^n}\), with units \(\mathrm{mol^{1-n}\ L^{n-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

The units of \(k\) and of the rate agree only when the concentration term disappears, that is when \(n = 0\) — so the Assertion holds, both being \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).

And the Reason states the same fact in words. Being independent of concentration means \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^0 = k\); the rate constant simply IS the rate, so the two must carry identical units.

[The marking scheme accepts BOTH the "correct explanation" answer and the "not the correct explanation" answer for this row. The case for the second reading is that the shared units and the independence of concentration are two statements of the same property rather than one causing the other.]

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Acetic acid but not formic acid can be halogenated in presence of red P and \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\).
Reason (R) : Acetic acid is a weaker acid than formic acid.
rows.context: For questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

The Assertion is correct. The Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction halogenates a carboxylic acid at its \(\alpha\) position, and formic acid has NO \(\alpha\) CARBON at all — its carboxyl group is attached directly to a hydrogen, so there is nothing to halogenate. Acetic acid has a methyl group there and reacts normally.

The Reason is also true. Acetic acid IS weaker than formic acid, \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 4.76 against 3.75, because its methyl group releases electron density and destabilises the anion.

But acid STRENGTH has nothing to do with the halogenation. The reaction proceeds through the ENOL of the acyl halide, and what it requires is an \(\alpha\) hydrogen — a structural feature, not an acidity. A stronger acid with an \(\alpha\) hydrogen would react perfectly well.

So the Reason states a true fact about the same two compounds and leaves the Assertion unexplained.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Trans \(\mathrm{[Cr\,Cl_2(ox)_2]^{3-}}\) shows optical isomerism.
Reason (R) : Optical isomerism is common in octahedral complexes involving didentate ligands.
rows.context: For questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE.

The TRANS isomer does NOT show optical isomerism. With the two chlorido ligands directly opposite each other, a plane of symmetry can be drawn containing both of them, with the two oxalate rings reflected across it. A species with a plane of symmetry is superimposable on its mirror image and cannot be optically active.

The CIS isomer is the one that is chiral: its two chlorides are adjacent, no plane can be found, and it exists as a pair of enantiomers.

The Reason is correct as a general statement. Optical isomerism IS common in octahedral complexes containing didentate ligands, because the chelate rings arrange themselves as a left or a right handed propeller — the tris-chelate complexes are always chiral for that reason.

But being common is not being universal, and the trans isomer named in the Assertion is exactly the case where the symmetry destroys it.

rows.stem:
(i) What should be the signs (positive/negative) for \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Cell}}\) and \(\Delta \mathrm{G^{\circ}}\) for a spontaneous redox reaction occurring under standard conditions ?
(ii) State Faraday's first law of electrolysis.
rows.solution:
(i) \(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}\) must be POSITIVE and \(\Delta \mathrm{G}^{\circ}\) must be NEGATIVE.

The two are linked by \(\Delta \mathrm{G}^{\circ} = -n\mathrm{F}E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}\), and both \(n\) and \(\mathrm{F}\) are positive quantities. The MINUS sign in that relation is what makes the two signs opposite: a positive cell potential forces a negative free energy change.

A negative \(\Delta \mathrm{G}^{\circ}\) is the thermodynamic condition for spontaneity, so the two statements say the same thing in different languages — one electrical, one thermodynamic.

(ii) FARADAY'S FIRST LAW OF ELECTROLYSIS states that the mass of a substance deposited or liberated at an electrode is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to the QUANTITY OF ELECTRICITY passed through the electrolyte:
\(w \propto \mathrm{Q}\), that is \(w = \mathrm{Z}\,\mathrm{Q} = \mathrm{Z}\,\mathrm{I}\,t\)

The constant \(\mathrm{Z}\) is the electrochemical equivalent of the substance, the mass deposited by one coulomb.

rows.stem:
Calculate the emf of the following cell at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Fe_{(s)}} \mid \mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\,(0.01\mathrm{M}) \parallel \mathrm{H^{+}_{(1M)}} \mid \mathrm{H_{2(g)}}\,(1\ \mathrm{bar}),\ \mathrm{Pt_{(s)}}\)
Given \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Cell}} = 0.44\) V.
rows.solution:
Read the cell diagram: iron is on the LEFT and so is the anode, oxidised to \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\); hydrogen ions are reduced at the right.

The cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Fe} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + \mathrm{H_2}\), so \(n = 2\). Solid iron does not appear in the quotient, and hydrogen at 1 bar contributes a factor of 1:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]^2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}44 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}01}{(1)^2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}44 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log 10^{-2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}44 + 0{\cdot}059\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}499\ \mathrm{V}\)

The direction of the shift is the check. Lowering the concentration of a PRODUCT ion makes the forward reaction more favourable by Le Chatelier's principle, so the measured emf must exceed the standard value — as it does, 0.499 against 0.44.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: What happens to the rate constant k and activation energy \(\mathrm{E_a}\) as the temperature of a chemical reaction is increased ? Justify.
rows.solution:
The rate constant \(k\) INCREASES; the activation energy \(E_a\) is UNCHANGED.

WHY \(k\) RISES. The Arrhenius equation gives \(k = \mathrm{A}e^{-E_a/\mathrm{RT}}\). Raising \(\mathrm{T}\) makes the exponent less negative, so the exponential grows and \(k\) with it. Physically, the fraction of molecules whose collisions carry at least \(E_a\) rises steeply with temperature — near room temperature a rise of ten degrees roughly DOUBLES the rate for a typical reaction.

WHY \(E_a\) DOES NOT CHANGE. The activation energy is the ENERGY BARRIER between the reactants and the activated complex, and it is fixed by the NATURE OF THE REACTANTS — which bonds must be stretched and which formed before the reaction can proceed. Heating the mixture supplies molecules with more energy to climb the barrier; it does not lower the barrier.

The distinction is worth holding onto. Only a CATALYST changes \(E_a\), by offering a different path with a lower barrier. Temperature changes how many molecules can clear the existing one.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem:
(a) Which of the following species cannot act as a ligand ? Give reason.
\(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\), \(\mathrm{NH_4^{+}}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{H_2O}\)
(b) The complex \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]Cl_2}\) is red in colour. Give IUPAC name of its linkage isomer.
rows.solution:
(a) The AMMONIUM ION, \(\mathrm{NH_4^+}\), cannot act as a ligand.

A ligand must DONATE an electron pair to the metal, so it needs a LONE PAIR available. The hydroxide ion has three on its oxygen, water has two, and methylamine has one on its nitrogen — all three can bind.

In the ammonium ion that lone pair is GONE. It has already been used to attach a fourth hydrogen, which is precisely how the ion forms from ammonia, so there is nothing left to donate.

The POSITIVE charge is a second objection: a positive species is repelled by a metal cation rather than drawn to it, which is why ligands are typically neutral molecules or anions.

(b) The linkage isomer is the one bound through the OTHER atom of the nitrite ion. Five ammines are neutral and the nitrite gives \(-1\) against two chlorides outside, so cobalt is \(+3\):
PENTAAMMINENITRITO-N-COBALT(III) CHLORIDE

[The two forms differ in colour, and the textbook assignment is that the NITRITO-O form is RED while the NITRITO-N form is YELLOW. The stem describes the given complex as red, which makes it the O-bonded one and its isomer the N-bonded one named above. The marking scheme instead answers "pentaamminenitrito-O-cobalt(III) chloride" — by that colour assignment, the red complex the question started from rather than its isomer.]

rows.stem: Why is boiling point of o-dichlorobenzene higher than p-dichlorobenzene but melting point of para isomer is higher than ortho isomer ?
rows.solution:
The two properties are governed by DIFFERENT things, which is why the two isomers change places.

BOILING POINT depends on the forces between molecules in the LIQUID, where there is no lattice, and there POLARITY decides. In the ortho isomer the two carbon-chlorine bond dipoles point in similar directions and reinforce each other, giving a net dipole moment; in the para isomer they point exactly OPPOSITE and cancel, leaving the molecule non-polar. The ortho isomer therefore has the stronger dipole-dipole attraction and the HIGHER boiling point.

MELTING POINT depends on the forces in the SOLID, where the molecules sit in a crystal lattice, and there PACKING decides. The para isomer is SYMMETRICAL, so its molecules fit closely and regularly into the lattice; more energy is needed to break that arrangement apart, and its melting point is HIGHER.

The general rule follows: among disubstituted benzenes the para isomer usually melts highest, being the best packer, while the ortho isomer usually boils highest, being the most polar.

rows.stem:
For the pair phenol and cyclohexanol, answer the following :
(a) Why is phenol more acidic than cyclohexanol ?
(b) Give one chemical test to distinguish between the two.
rows.solution:
(a) Because the PHENOXIDE ION is stabilised by RESONANCE.

Acidity is decided by the stability of the anion left behind. When phenol loses its proton, the negative charge on the oxygen is DELOCALISED into the ring, spreading to the ortho and para carbons, so it is not concentrated on one atom.

The cyclohexoxide ion has no such relief. Its ring is saturated, with no \(\pi\) system to accept the charge, so the whole of it stays on the oxygen. A concentrated charge is less stable.

There is a second contribution. The phenol carbon bearing the hydroxyl is \(sp^2\) and so more electronegative than the \(sp^3\) carbon of cyclohexanol, which helps pull density away from the oxygen even before the proton leaves.

The difference is large: phenol has \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 10 against cyclohexanol's 18, a factor of a hundred million in acid strength.

(b) Add NEUTRAL FERRIC CHLORIDE solution to each. PHENOL gives a VIOLET colouration, forming a coloured iron complex; CYCLOHEXANOL gives no colour at all.

The test works for phenols generally and not for ordinary alcohols. Sodium hydroxide would serve too: phenol dissolves to give sodium phenoxide, while cyclohexanol does not react.

rows.stem:
(i) Draw the zwitter ion structure for sulphanilic acid.
(ii) How can the activating effect of \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group in aniline be controlled ?
rows.solution:
(i) Sulphanilic acid exists as a ZWITTER ION — an internal salt, with both a positive and a negative centre in the same molecule and no net charge.

The sulphonic acid group is strongly acidic and gives up its proton; the amino group is basic and accepts it. The proton simply moves from one end of the molecule to the other:
\(\mathrm{{}^+H_3N{-}C_6H_4{-}SO_3^-}\)

The structure is a benzene ring carrying \(-\overset{+}{\mathrm{N}}\mathrm{H_3}\) at one position and \(-\mathrm{SO_3^-}\) PARA to it.

Two observations confirm it: sulphanilic acid is a high melting solid, insoluble in organic solvents but soluble in water, exactly as an ionic compound should be.

(ii) By ACETYLATION — treating aniline with acetic anhydride to give ACETANILIDE, and removing the acetyl group by hydrolysis afterwards.

In acetanilide the nitrogen's lone pair is shared with the neighbouring CARBONYL group, which competes with the ring for it. Less density reaches the ring, so the group remains ortho, para directing but is much LESS activating.

That is what makes a controlled reaction possible: bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline with aniline itself, but with acetanilide it gives the mono-substituted para product, and acid or alkaline hydrolysis then returns the free amine.

rows.stem:
(i) Complete the reaction with the main product formed :
benzenediazonium chloride \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}}\)
(ii) Convert Bromoethane to Propanamine.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — sub-part (i)'s reactant is DRAWN as a benzene ring carrying \(\mathrm{N_2^{+}Cl^{-}}\), with \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\) written over the reaction arrow. Naming it 'benzenediazonium chloride' is a lossless reading of the drawing and does not state the answer (the product is what is asked for), so the stem is answerable from text alone and this is illustrative rather than required. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(i) Ethanol REDUCES the diazonium salt, replacing the diazonium group by HYDROGEN:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The main product is BENZENE, with ethanol itself oxidised to ethanal. Hypophosphorous acid does the same job and is the cleaner reagent for it.

The reaction matters in synthesis: it lets an amino group be used to DIRECT a substitution and then be removed entirely, which is how substitution patterns are reached that could not be obtained directly.

(ii) BROMOETHANE TO PROPANAMINE, in two steps. Count the carbons — two in, three out — so a carbon must be ADDED, and cyanide is what adds it:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Br} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KCN}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CN} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}\)

The cyanide substitutes for bromide, and reduction of the nitrile gives the primary amine with the carbon count unchanged.

The reagent must be potassium CYANIDE, not silver cyanide: the silver salt is largely covalent and its nitrogen attacks instead, giving the isocyanide.

rows.stem: Give the reaction of glucose with hydrogen cyanide. Presence of which group is confirmed by this reaction ?
rows.solution:
Hydrogen cyanide ADDS across the carbonyl group of glucose, giving the CYANOHYDRIN:
\(\mathrm{CH_2OH{-}(CHOH)_4{-}CHO} + \mathrm{HCN} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_2OH{-}(CHOH)_4{-}CH(OH)(CN)}\)

The product is glucose cyanohydrin, with SEVEN carbons where glucose had six.

The reaction confirms the presence of a CARBONYL group — the \(>\mathrm{C{=}O}\) of an aldehyde. Nucleophilic addition of this kind is characteristic of the carbonyl group and of nothing else in the molecule; the several hydroxyl groups do not react with hydrogen cyanide at all.

It is one of the classical proofs of glucose's structure, and it fits with the others: glucose forms an oxime with hydroxylamine, also a carbonyl reaction, and reduces Tollens' reagent, which narrows the carbonyl down to an ALDEHYDE rather than a ketone.

rows.stem:
(a) For the reaction
\(2\mathrm{N_2O_{5(g)}} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{NO_{2(g)}} + \mathrm{O_{2(g)}}\) at 318 K
calculate the rate of reaction if rate of disappearance of \(\mathrm{N_2O_{5(g)}}\) is \(1.4 \times 10^{-3}\) m \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\).
(b) For a first order reaction derive the relationship \(\mathrm{t_{99\%}} = 2\mathrm{t_{90\%}}\)
rows.solution:
(a) The RATE OF REACTION is one number describing the whole process, obtained by dividing each species' own rate by its coefficient:
\(\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]}{\Delta t} = +\dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{NO_2}]}{\Delta t} = +\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{O_2}]}{\Delta t}\)

Substituting the rate of disappearance of \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\):
\(\text{Rate} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(\text{Rate} = 7 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{M\ s^{-1}}\)

The division is what makes the answer unambiguous: without it, the same reaction would have four different "rates" depending on which species was watched.

(b) For a first order reaction the time to reach any fraction is
\(t = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\)

When 99% has reacted, 1% remains, so the ratio is \(100/1\):
\(t_{99\%} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log 100 = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k} \times 2\)

When 90% has reacted, 10% remains, so the ratio is \(100/10\):
\(t_{90\%} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log 10 = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k} \times 1\)

Dividing one by the other, every constant cancels:
\(\dfrac{t_{99\%}}{t_{90\%}} = \dfrac{\log 100}{\log 10} = \dfrac{2}{1} = 2\), so \(t_{99\%} = 2\,t_{90\%}\)

The result is independent of \(k\), so it holds for EVERY first order reaction. The reason is that first order decay falls by a constant FACTOR in equal times: the amount drops to a tenth in one interval, and to a tenth of THAT in a second equal interval.

rows.stem:
(a) On the basis of crystal field theory write the electronic configuration for \(\mathrm{d^5}\) ion with a strong field ligand for which \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\).
(b) \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) has tetrahedral geometry while \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\) has square planar yet both exhibit dimagnetism. Explain.
[Atomic number : Ni = 28]
rows.solution:
(a) The configuration is \(t_{2g}^5\,e_g^0\).

In an octahedral field the five d orbitals split into a lower set of three, \(t_{2g}\), and an upper set of two, \(e_g\), separated by \(\Delta_0\). Each electron entering must choose between two costs: going to the upper set costs \(\Delta_0\), while pairing in the lower set costs the pairing energy \(\mathrm{P}\).

The question specifies \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\) — a STRONG FIELD — so pairing is the cheaper option, and the electrons fill the lower set completely before any reaches the upper one.

Five electrons therefore sit entirely in the three lower orbitals, as two pairs and one single, leaving \(e_g\) empty. This is a LOW SPIN complex with ONE unpaired electron, \(\mu = 1{\cdot}73\) B.M.

A WEAK field, with \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\), would have given \(t_{2g}^3\,e_g^2\) — all five unpaired, \(\mu = 5{\cdot}92\) B.M. The same ion gives opposite magnetic behaviour depending only on the ligand.

(b) The two differ in GEOMETRY but agree in having NO UNPAIRED ELECTRONS, which is what diamagnetism requires.

In \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) nickel is in the ZERO oxidation state, \(3d^8 4s^2\). Carbon monoxide drives the two \(4s\) electrons into the d set, giving \(3d^{10}\) — completely full, every electron paired, and no \(3d\) orbital vacant. Bonding must then use the \(4s\) and three \(4p\) orbitals, giving \(sp^3\) and a TETRAHEDRAL shape.

In \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\) nickel is \(+2\), that is \(3d^8\). Cyanide is a strong field ligand and forces those eight electrons into FOUR of the five d orbitals as four pairs, which FREES one \(3d\) orbital. That orbital with the \(4s\) and two \(4p\) gives \(dsp^2\) and a SQUARE PLANAR shape.

So one reaches a full d subshell and the other a rearranged one, but in both cases every electron is paired.

rows.stem:
(a) Illustrate Sandmeyer's reaction with an equation.
(b) Explain, why \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH}\) is more basic than \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\) in aqueous solution.
rows.solution:
(a) SANDMEYER'S REACTION replaces the diazonium group by a halogen or a cyano group, using the corresponding COPPER(I) salt:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CuCl}/\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

The same reaction with copper(I) bromide in hydrobromic acid gives bromobenzene, and with copper(I) cyanide in potassium cyanide it gives cyanobenzene.

Its value lies in doing what direct halogenation cannot. Chlorinating benzene gives a mixture and cannot be steered; this route lets a substituent be placed EXACTLY where the amino group stood, since the diazonium group simply leaves as nitrogen from that position.

(b) Because of SOLVATION and STERIC HINDRANCE, which both favour the secondary amine in water.

Two effects compete. Each methyl group RELEASES electron density to the nitrogen, making the lone pair more available — on this count alone the tertiary amine should be the stronger base.

But in AQUEOUS solution the CONJUGATE ACID must be stabilised by hydrogen bonding to water, and that needs hydrogens on the nitrogen. The dimethylammonium ion has TWO; the trimethylammonium ion has only ONE, so it is far less well hydrated.

The three methyl groups of the tertiary amine also CROWD the nitrogen and obstruct the approach of a proton.

The two disadvantages together outweigh the inductive advantage, so dimethylamine is the stronger base in water. In the GAS PHASE, where no solvent can hydrogen bond, the order reverses and trimethylamine is the strongest.

rows.stem:
Give reasons for any 3 of the following observations :
(a) Penta-acetate of glucose does not react with hydroxylamine.
(b) Amino acids behave like salts.
(c) Water soluble vitamins must be taken regularly in diet.
(d) The two strands in DNA are complimentary to each other.
rows.solution:
(a) Because the penta-acetate has NO FREE ANOMERIC HYDROXYL, so its ring cannot open.

Glucose reacts with hydroxylamine only because a small fraction of it exists in the OPEN CHAIN form, carrying a genuine aldehyde group, and it is that form the reagent attacks. The equilibrium then draws more of the ring form across.

Acetylating all five hydroxyls locks the anomeric one as an ester. The ring can no longer open, no aldehyde is ever present, and no oxime forms.

This is one of the observations that showed glucose does NOT contain a free aldehyde group at all times — a key step towards the cyclic structure.

(b) Because they exist as ZWITTER IONS.

An amino acid carries an acidic carboxyl group and a basic amino group in the same molecule, and the proton simply moves from one to the other, giving \(\mathrm{{}^+H_3N{-}CHR{-}COO^-}\) — an internal salt.

Its properties are then those of an ionic compound: high melting points, solubility in water and insolubility in organic solvents, and low volatility.

(c) Because they are NOT STORED in the body.

Water soluble vitamins — vitamin C and the B group — dissolve in the body's aqueous fluids, so any excess is EXCRETED in the urine and no reserve accumulates. They must therefore be supplied regularly in the diet, and a few weeks without vitamin C is enough to bring on scurvy.

Fat soluble vitamins behave oppositely, being stored in the liver and in adipose tissue, so they need not be taken daily.

(d) Because the bases PAIR SPECIFICALLY through hydrogen bonds.

Adenine pairs only with thymine, through TWO hydrogen bonds; guanine pairs only with cytosine, through THREE. The pairing is fixed by the sizes and the positions of the donor and acceptor groups — a purine must face a pyrimidine for the two strands to stay a constant distance apart.

So the sequence of one strand DETERMINES the other completely, which is what makes replication possible: each strand serves as the template for its partner.

rows.stem:
(i) Why is the C – O bond length in phenols less than that in methanol ?
(ii) Arrange the following in order of increasing boiling point :
Ethoxyethane, Butanal, Butanol, n-butane
(iii) How can phenol be prepared from anisole ? Give reaction.
rows.solution:
(i) Because the carbon-oxygen bond in phenol has PARTIAL DOUBLE BOND CHARACTER.

The oxygen's lone pair is DELOCALISED into the benzene ring, and the resonance structures that result place a double bond between the carbon and the oxygen. A bond with double bond character is shorter and stronger than a pure single bond.

A second reason reinforces it: the carbon bearing the hydroxyl is \(sp^2\) in phenol but \(sp^3\) in methanol, and an \(sp^2\) orbital has more s character, so it is smaller and forms a shorter bond.

The measured values are 136 pm in phenol against 142 pm in methanol.

The same delocalisation explains why phenol's \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bond does not break easily, so phenol cannot be converted to a halide by hydrogen halides the way an alcohol can.

(ii) Increasing boiling point:
N-BUTANE < ETHOXYETHANE < BUTANAL < BUTANOL

All four have comparable molar masses, so the order is set entirely by the INTERMOLECULAR FORCES.

n-Butane is non-polar and has only weak dispersion forces. Ethoxyethane is slightly polar but its oxygen is flanked by two alkyl groups and it has no \(\mathrm{O-H}\), so it cannot hydrogen bond to itself. Butanal is more polar still, its carbonyl group giving stronger dipole-dipole attraction. Butanol alone has an \(\mathrm{O-H}\) group and forms HYDROGEN BONDS, much the strongest of these forces, so it boils highest.

(iii) Anisole is cleaved by a hydrogen halide, the attack falling on the METHYL carbon:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}O{-}CH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_3I}\)

The products are PHENOL and iodomethane. The bond from oxygen to the RING carbon survives, having partial double bond character as described above, and a ring carbon is not open to backside attack in any case — so iodobenzene and methanol are never formed.

rows.stem:
(i) Give mechanism of the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \xrightarrow[413\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2 - O - CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
(ii) Illustrate hydroboration – oxidation reaction with an example.
rows.solution:
(i) MECHANISM OF ETHER FORMATION AT 413 K, in three steps.

STEP 1 — protonation of the alcohol. The oxygen picks up a proton, converting the poor leaving group \(-\mathrm{OH}\) into the good one, water:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\ddot{O}H} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}H_2}\)

STEP 2 — nucleophilic attack. A SECOND alcohol molecule, still unprotonated, attacks the carbon of the protonated one and displaces water. This is the SLOW step and it proceeds by \(\mathrm{S_N}2\):
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\ddot{O}H} + \mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}H_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}(H){-}CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

STEP 3 — loss of a proton, which regenerates the catalyst:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}(H){-}CH_2CH_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}O{-}CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{H^+}\)

The TEMPERATURE decides the product. At 413 K there is plenty of unreacted alcohol available to act as the nucleophile and the ether forms; at 443 K the protonated alcohol instead loses water to a carbocation and eliminates, giving ethene.

(ii) HYDROBORATION-OXIDATION adds water across a double bond with ANTI-MARKOVNIKOV orientation. Diborane adds first, the electron deficient boron attaching to the LESS substituted carbon; alkaline hydrogen peroxide then replaces the boron by a hydroxyl in the same position:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{B_2H_6}} (\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2})_3\mathrm{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O_2}/\mathrm{OH^-}} 3\,\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}\)

Propene gives PROPAN-1-OL, where acid catalysed hydration would have given propan-2-ol.

rows.stem: Why racemisation occurs in \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) ?
rows.context:
Nucleophilic Substitution reaction of haloalkane can be conducted according to both \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) and \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) mechanisms. \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) is a two step reaction while \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) is a single step reaction. For any haloalkane which mechanism is followed depends on factors such as structure of haloalkane, properties of leaving group, nucleophilic reagent and solvent.
Influences of solvent polarity : In \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction, the polarity of the system increases from the reactant to the transition state, because a polar solvent has a greater effect on the transition state than the reactant, thereby reducing activation energy and accelerating the reaction. In \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, the polarity of the system generally does not change from the reactant to the transition state and only charge dispersion occurs. At this time, polar solvent has a great stabilizing effect on Nu than the transition state, thereby increasing activation energy and slow down the reaction rate. For example, the decomposition rate \((\mathrm{S_N}1)\) of tertiary chlorobutane at 25 °C in water (dielectric constant 79) is 300000 times faster than in ethanol (dielectric constant 24). The reaction rate \((\mathrm{S_N}2)\) of 2-Bromopropane and NaOH in ethanol containing 40% water is twice slower than in absolute ethanol. Hence the level of solvent polarity has influence on both \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) and \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, but with different results. Generally speaking weak polar solvent is favourable for \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, while strong polar solvent is favourable for \(\mathrm{S_N}1\). Generally speaking the substitution reaction of tertiary haloalkane is based on \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) mechanism in solvents with a strong polarity (for example ethanol containing water).
rows.solution:
Because the intermediate CARBOCATION is PLANAR.

An \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction proceeds in two steps. The leaving group departs first, and the carbon left behind becomes \(sp^2\) HYBRIDISED, with its three remaining groups in a plane and an empty p orbital perpendicular to it.

That flat intermediate has TWO IDENTICAL FACES. The nucleophile can attack from either side with equal ease — from the face the leaving group vacated, giving RETENTION of configuration, or from the opposite face, giving INVERSION.

Both products form, and in roughly equal amounts, so an optically pure starting material yields a nearly RACEMIC mixture whose rotations cancel.

The contrast with \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) is the point. There the nucleophile attacks from BEHIND the leaving group in a single step, so only one face is available and the product shows complete INVERSION rather than racemisation.

Generally speaking the substitution reaction of tertiary haloalkane is based on \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) mechanism in solvents with a strong polarity (for example ethanol containing water).
rows.solution:
Because the ETHYL GROUP releases electron density towards the oxygen.

Polarity in these molecules comes from the \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond and from the oxygen's lone pairs. In water the oxygen is flanked by two HYDROGENS, which have no electron releasing effect, so the oxygen's pull on the bonding electrons is undiminished.

In ethanol one hydrogen has been replaced by an ETHYL group, which pushes electron density towards the oxygen by the \(+\mathrm{I}\) effect. That partly offsets the oxygen's own electronegativity, reducing the charge separation and so the polarity.

The bulk of the ethyl group also matters: it is a hydrocarbon portion, non-polar in itself, so it dilutes the polar character of the molecule as a whole.

The dielectric constants record the difference — about 79 for water against 24 for ethanol — and that gap is exactly what the case study uses, water accelerating an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) decomposition 300000-fold relative to ethanol.

rows.stem:
Which one of the following in each pair is more reactive towards \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction ?
(i) \(\mathrm{CH_3 - CH_2 - I}\) or \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2 - Cl}\)
(ii) a six-membered carbon ring bearing \(-\mathrm{Cl}\) or a six-membered carbon ring bearing \(-\mathrm{CH_2 - Cl}\)

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — sub-part (ii)'s two compounds are DRAWN and are PLAIN HEXAGONS: no inner aromatic circle and no double bonds. Adjudicated 2026-09-12 against 56/5/1's own printed page AND its own marking scheme, which draws the answer as the same plain hexagon bearing -CH2-Cl. They are therefore NOT nameable as chlorobenzene / benzyl chloride, so the stem describes rather than names and the crop must be attached. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
(i) IODOETHANE is more reactive.

In any nucleophilic substitution the carbon-halogen bond must BREAK, so the weaker bond reacts faster. The \(\mathrm{C-I}\) bond enthalpy is about 238 kJ per mole against the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond's 339, making iodine much the better LEAVING GROUP.

Two reasons lie behind that: the iodine atom is large, so its orbital overlaps carbon's poorly and the bond is long and weak; and the iodide ion, with its charge spread over a large volume, is the more stable anion.

(ii) The ring bearing \(-\mathrm{CH_2{-}Cl}\) is more reactive — cyclohexylmethyl chloride rather than chlorocyclohexane.

An \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction needs the nucleophile to reach the carbon from BEHIND the leaving group, so the less crowded that carbon is, the faster the reaction. In cyclohexylmethyl chloride the chlorine sits on a PRIMARY \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) carbon, attached to just one other carbon and open on the other side.

In chlorocyclohexane the chlorine is on a RING carbon, which is SECONDARY and flanked by the rest of the ring, so the backside approach is obstructed.

The general \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) order follows from the same reasoning: methyl > primary > secondary > tertiary.

rows.stem:
Arrange the following in the increasing order of their reactivity towards \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reactions :
(i) 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, 1-Bromopentane, 2-Bromopentane
(ii) 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane, 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane
rows.context:
Nucleophilic Substitution reaction of haloalkane can be conducted according to both \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) and \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) mechanisms. \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) is a two step reaction while \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) is a single step reaction. For any haloalkane which mechanism is followed depends on factors such as structure of haloalkane, properties of leaving group, nucleophilic reagent and solvent.
Influences of solvent polarity : In \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction, the polarity of the system increases from the reactant to the transition state, because a polar solvent has a greater effect on the transition state than the reactant, thereby reducing activation energy and accelerating the reaction. In \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, the polarity of the system generally does not change from the reactant to the transition state and only charge dispersion occurs. At this time, polar solvent has a great stabilizing effect on Nu than the transition state, thereby increasing activation energy and slow down the reaction rate. For example, the decomposition rate \((\mathrm{S_N}1)\) of tertiary chlorobutane at 25 °C in water (dielectric constant 79) is 300000 times faster than in ethanol (dielectric constant 24). The reaction rate \((\mathrm{S_N}2)\) of 2-Bromopropane and NaOH in ethanol containing 40% water is twice slower than in absolute ethanol. Hence the level of solvent polarity has influence on both \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) and \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, but with different results. Generally speaking weak polar solvent is favourable for \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, while strong polar solvent is favourable for \(\mathrm{S_N}1\). Generally speaking the substitution reaction of tertiary haloalkane is based on \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) mechanism in solvents with a strong polarity (for example ethanol containing water).
rows.solution:
Reactivity towards \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) is decided by the stability of the CARBOCATION formed when the halide leaves, because that formation is the slow step. Alkyl groups stabilise a positive charge, so the order runs primary < secondary < tertiary.

(i) 1-BROMOPENTANE < 2-BROMOPENTANE < 2-BROMO-2-METHYLBUTANE

The first is primary, its cation carrying no stabilisation at all. The second is secondary. The third is TERTIARY, its cation flanked by three alkyl groups.

(ii) 1-BROMO-3-METHYLBUTANE < 2-BROMO-3-METHYLBUTANE < 2-BROMO-2-METHYLBUTANE

The branch at position 3 does not matter here — what counts is the carbon actually BEARING the bromine. In the first compound that carbon is primary, in the second secondary, in the third tertiary.

Reading the name is enough in both parts: locate the carbon carrying the halogen and count how many other carbons it is attached to. The \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) order would be exactly the REVERSE of these, since crowding hinders backside attack.

rows.stem: Why does conductivity decrease with dilution ?
rows.context:
Rahul set-up an experiment to find resistance of aqueous KCl solution for different concentrations at 298 K using a conductivity cell connected to a Wheatstone bridge. He fed the Wheatstone bridge with a.c. power in the audio frequency range 550 to 5000 cycles per second. Once the resistance was calculated from null point he also calculated the conductivity K and molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) and recorded his readings in tabular form.

| S.No. | Conc.(M) | k S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) | \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. | 1.00 | \(111.3 \times 10^{-3}\) | 111.3 |
| 2. | 0.10 | \(12.9 \times 10^{-3}\) | 129.0 |
| 3. | 0.01 | \(1.41 \times 10^{-3}\) | 141.0 |
rows.solution:
Because CONDUCTIVITY is measured for a FIXED VOLUME, and dilution puts FEWER IONS into that volume.

Conductivity is the conductance of a solution held between two electrodes one centimetre apart with an area of one square centimetre — a fixed block of solution. What carries the current through it is the IONS it contains, so the conductivity depends on how many ions are present PER UNIT VOLUME.

Diluting spreads the same ions through more solution, so that fixed block now holds fewer of them and conducts less. Rahul's own table shows it: \(\kappa\) falls from \(111{\cdot}3 \times 10^{-3}\) to \(1{\cdot}41 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\) as the concentration drops from 1.00 M to 0.01 M.

MOLAR conductivity behaves the OPPOSITE way, rising from 111.3 to 141.0 over the same range, because it counts the conductance furnished by a fixed AMOUNT of electrolyte rather than a fixed volume — and those ions, now further apart, interfere with one another less.

rows.stem: If \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}\) of KCl is 150.0 S \(\mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\), calculate the degree of dissociation of 0.01 M KCl.
rows.context:
Rahul set-up an experiment to find resistance of aqueous KCl solution for different concentrations at 298 K using a conductivity cell connected to a Wheatstone bridge. He fed the Wheatstone bridge with a.c. power in the audio frequency range 550 to 5000 cycles per second. Once the resistance was calculated from null point he also calculated the conductivity K and molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) and recorded his readings in tabular form.

| S.No. | Conc.(M) | k S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) | \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. | 1.00 | \(111.3 \times 10^{-3}\) | 111.3 |
| 2. | 0.10 | \(12.9 \times 10^{-3}\) | 129.0 |
| 3. | 0.01 | \(1.41 \times 10^{-3}\) | 141.0 |
rows.solution:
The degree of dissociation is the ratio of the measured molar conductivity to the limiting value:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}}\)

From Rahul's table, the 0.01 M solution has \(\Lambda_m = 141{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\), and the limiting value is given as \(150{\cdot}0\):
\(\alpha = \dfrac{141{\cdot}0}{150{\cdot}0}\)

\(\alpha = 0{\cdot}94\), that is 94% dissociated

The ratio must lie between 0 and 1, which is the check on the arithmetic.

Strictly this treatment belongs to a WEAK electrolyte, where the shortfall genuinely measures incomplete dissociation. Potassium chloride is a STRONG electrolyte and is fully dissociated at every dilution; its shortfall is caused by the ions interfering with one another's movement, so the 0.94 is better read as a "conductance ratio" than as a true degree of dissociation.

rows.stem: If Rahul had used HCl instead to KCl then would you expect the \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) values to be more or less than those per KCl for a given concentration. Justify.
rows.context:
Rahul set-up an experiment to find resistance of aqueous KCl solution for different concentrations at 298 K using a conductivity cell connected to a Wheatstone bridge. He fed the Wheatstone bridge with a.c. power in the audio frequency range 550 to 5000 cycles per second. Once the resistance was calculated from null point he also calculated the conductivity K and molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) and recorded his readings in tabular form.

| S.No. | Conc.(M) | k S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) | \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. | 1.00 | \(111.3 \times 10^{-3}\) | 111.3 |
| 2. | 0.10 | \(12.9 \times 10^{-3}\) | 129.0 |
| 3. | 0.01 | \(1.41 \times 10^{-3}\) | 141.0 |
rows.solution:
The \(\Lambda_m\) values for hydrochloric acid would be MORE than those for potassium chloride at the same concentration.

Both are strong electrolytes giving two ions per formula unit, and both share the chloride ion, so the comparison comes down to \(\mathrm{H^+}\) against \(\mathrm{K^+}\).

The HYDROGEN ION conducts far better than any other ion, because it does not have to travel bodily through the solution. It moves by a PROTON JUMP along the hydrogen bonded network of water molecules — a proton attaches to one water molecule while another leaves the far side — so charge crosses the solution much faster than any ion could migrate. The limiting ionic conductivities record it: about 349.6 for \(\mathrm{H^+}\) against 73.5 for \(\mathrm{K^+}\).

[The marking scheme adds a note that the DATA GIVEN IN THE PAPER does not support this answer, and directs full marks for any attempt. The table records potassium chloride alone, so nothing in the experiment lets the two electrolytes be compared — the answer has to come from knowledge of ionic mobilities rather than from Rahul's readings.]

rows.stem: Amit, a classmate of Rahul repeated the same experiment with \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) solution instead of KCl solution. Give one point that would be similar and one that would be different in his observations as compared to Rahul.
rows.context:
Rahul set-up an experiment to find resistance of aqueous KCl solution for different concentrations at 298 K using a conductivity cell connected to a Wheatstone bridge. He fed the Wheatstone bridge with a.c. power in the audio frequency range 550 to 5000 cycles per second. Once the resistance was calculated from null point he also calculated the conductivity K and molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) and recorded his readings in tabular form.

| S.No. | Conc.(M) | k S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) | \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. | 1.00 | \(111.3 \times 10^{-3}\) | 111.3 |
| 2. | 0.10 | \(12.9 \times 10^{-3}\) | 129.0 |
| 3. | 0.01 | \(1.41 \times 10^{-3}\) | 141.0 |
rows.solution:
SIMILARITY: in both cases the MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY INCREASES on dilution, while the CONDUCTIVITY itself decreases.

DIFFERENCE: the SHAPE of the increase, and what can be done with it.

For potassium chloride, a STRONG electrolyte, \(\Lambda_m\) rises only GRADUALLY — the salt is fully dissociated at every dilution, and the small rise merely reflects the ions interfering with one another less as they move apart. A plot against \(\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\) is very nearly a straight line, so extrapolating it to zero concentration gives \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) directly.

For acetic acid, a WEAK electrolyte, \(\Lambda_m\) rises STEEPLY, and steepest of all near infinite dilution. The cause is different: the DEGREE OF DISSOCIATION itself is increasing, so one mole of acid is furnishing more and more ions. The curve never straightens and never meets the axis, so \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) cannot be obtained by extrapolation at all and must be calculated from KOHLRAUSCH'S LAW instead.

Amit's absolute values would also be much LOWER than Rahul's, acetic acid being only slightly ionised at ordinary concentrations.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
(i) Why is boiling point of 1M NaCl solution more than that of 1M glucose solution ?
(ii) A non-volatile solute 'X' (molar mass = 50 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) when dissolved in 78g of benzene reduced its vapour pressure to 90%. Calculate the mass of X dissolved in the solution.
(iii) Calculate the boiling point elevation for a solution prepared by adding 10g of \(\mathrm{MgCl_2}\) to 200g of water assuming \(\mathrm{MgCl_2}\) is completely dissociated.
(\(\mathrm{K_b}\) for Water = 0.512 K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), Molar mass \(\mathrm{MgCl_2}\) = 95g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
(i) Because sodium chloride DISSOCIATES and glucose does not.

Elevation of boiling point is a COLLIGATIVE property, so it depends on the NUMBER OF PARTICLES, not on what they are.

One mole of glucose gives one mole of particles; its van't Hoff factor is 1. One mole of sodium chloride gives \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), that is TWO moles of particles, so \(i = 2\).

At the same molarity the salt therefore produces about TWICE the elevation, and its solution boils higher.

(ii) The vapour pressure falls to 90% of its original value, so \(p = 0{\cdot}9\,p^{\circ}\) and the relative lowering is \(0{\cdot}1\):
\(\dfrac{p^{\circ} - p}{p^{\circ}} = x_2 = \dfrac{n_2}{n_2 + n_1}\)

Benzene has molar mass 78, so \(n_1 = 78/78 = 1\) mole. With \(n_2 = w/50\):
\(0{\cdot}1 = \dfrac{w/50}{(w/50) + 1}\)
\(0{\cdot}1\left(\dfrac{w}{50} + 1\right) = \dfrac{w}{50}\)
\(0{\cdot}1 = 0{\cdot}9 \times \dfrac{w}{50}\), so \(\dfrac{w}{50} = 0{\cdot}1111\)

\(w = 5{\cdot}55\ \mathrm{g}\)

(Taking the dilute approximation \(x_2 \approx n_2/n_1\) gives 5 g, which the marking scheme also accepts.)

(iii) Magnesium chloride dissociates into three ions, so \(i = 3\):
\(\Delta \mathrm{T_b} = i\,\mathrm{K_b}\,m = 3 \times 0{\cdot}512 \times \dfrac{10}{95} \times \dfrac{1000}{200}\)

The molality is \(\frac{10}{95} \times \frac{1000}{200} = 0{\cdot}526\) mol per kg:
\(\Delta \mathrm{T_b} = 3 \times 0{\cdot}512 \times 0{\cdot}526\)

\(\Delta \mathrm{T_b} = 0{\cdot}81\ \mathrm{K}\)

Note that molality uses the mass of the SOLVENT alone, 200 g, not the mass of the solution.

rows.stem:
(i) Why is the value of Van't Hoff factor for ethanoic acid in benzene close to 0.5 ?
(ii) Determine the osmotic pressure of a solution prepared by dissolving \(2.32 \times 10^{-2}\)g of \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\) in 2L of solution at 25 °C, assuming that \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\) is completely dissociated.
(R = 0.082 L atm \(\mathrm{K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), Molar mass \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\) = 174g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
(iii) When 25.6g of Sulphur was dissolved in 1000g of benzene, the freezing point lowered by 0.512 K. Calculate the formula of Sulphur \((\mathrm{S}_x)\).
(\(\mathrm{K_f}\) for benzene = 5.12 K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), Atomic mass of Sulphur = 32g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
(i) Because ethanoic acid DIMERISES in benzene, halving the number of particles.

Two molecules join through a PAIR of hydrogen bonds, each carboxyl group donating its \(\mathrm{O-H}\) to the other's carbonyl oxygen, closing an eight-membered ring. Benzene is non-polar and cannot compete for those hydrogen bonds, so the dimer survives intact in it.

With essentially every molecule paired, the observed particle count is half the expected one:
\(i = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0{\cdot}5\)

In WATER the value would be close to 1 or a little above, water breaking up the dimer by hydrogen bonding to each molecule separately, and the acid ionising slightly besides. The van't Hoff factor is therefore a property of the solute AND the solvent together, never of the solute alone.

(ii) Potassium sulphate gives three ions, so \(i = 3\). The concentration is \(\frac{2{\cdot}32 \times 10^{-2}}{174}\) moles in 2 L:
\(\pi = i\,\mathrm{C}\,\mathrm{R}\,\mathrm{T} = 3 \times \dfrac{2{\cdot}32 \times 10^{-2}}{174 \times 2} \times 0{\cdot}082 \times 298\)

The concentration works out as \(6{\cdot}67 \times 10^{-5}\) mol per litre:
\(\pi = 3 \times 6{\cdot}67 \times 10^{-5} \times 24{\cdot}44\)

\(\pi = 4{\cdot}88 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{atm}\)

The temperature must be converted to kelvin, 298 K, and the volume expressed in litres.

(iii) Find the molar mass from the freezing point depression, then divide by the atomic mass:
\(\Delta \mathrm{T_f} = \mathrm{K_f} \times \dfrac{w_2}{\mathrm{M_2}} \times \dfrac{1000}{w_1}\)
\(0{\cdot}512 = 5{\cdot}12 \times \dfrac{25{\cdot}6}{\mathrm{M_2}} \times \dfrac{1000}{1000}\)

\(\mathrm{M_2} = \dfrac{5{\cdot}12 \times 25{\cdot}6}{0{\cdot}512} = 256\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Since each sulphur atom weighs 32:
\(32x = 256\), so \(x = 8\)

The formula is \(\mathrm{S_8}\) — the puckered crown-shaped ring, which is how sulphur exists in the solid and in solution in benzene.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Write the reaction involved in Cannizaro's reaction.
(ii) Why are the boiling point of aldehydes and ketones lower than that of corresponding carboxylic acids ?
(iii) An organic compound 'A' with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_5H_8O_2}\) is reduced to n-pentane with hydrazine followed by heating with NaOH and Glycol. 'A' forms a dioxime with hydroxylamine and gives a positive Iodoform and Tollen's test. Identify 'A' and give its reaction for Iodoform and Tollen's test.
rows.solution:
(i) CANNIZZARO'S REACTION is a disproportionation of an aldehyde having NO \(\alpha\) HYDROGEN, treated with concentrated alkali. One molecule is oxidised to the salt of an acid and another reduced to an alcohol:
\(2\,\mathrm{HCHO} + \mathrm{KOH\ (conc.)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3OH} + \mathrm{HCOOK}\)

Benzaldehyde behaves the same way, giving benzyl alcohol and potassium benzoate. The absence of an \(\alpha\) hydrogen is what makes this route available — an aldehyde that has one undergoes the aldol condensation instead.

(ii) Because carboxylic acids form STRONG HYDROGEN BONDS while aldehydes and ketones have only DIPOLE-DIPOLE attraction.

A carboxylic acid has an \(\mathrm{O-H}\) group, so two molecules associate through a PAIR of hydrogen bonds into a dimer. Breaking that dimer costs a great deal of energy, and it must be broken before the molecules can enter the vapour.

An aldehyde or ketone has no \(\mathrm{O-H}\) at all. Its carbonyl group is polar, so the molecules attract one another by dipole-dipole forces, but these are far weaker than hydrogen bonds. Their boiling points sit between those of the corresponding alkanes and alcohols.

(iii) Take the four clues in turn. Reduction to N-PENTANE by the Wolff-Kishner method converts every carbonyl to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\), so the skeleton is a STRAIGHT chain of five carbons. A DIOXIME means TWO carbonyl groups, which the formula's two oxygens confirm. A positive IODOFORM test requires a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group; a positive TOLLENS' test requires an ALDEHYDE.

The only arrangement satisfying all four is
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3{-}CO{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CHO}\), 4-oxopentanal

IODOFORM TEST — the methyl ketone end is attacked, giving the yellow precipitate:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_2CHO} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{I_2}/\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{CHI_3}\downarrow + \text{the carboxylate}\)

TOLLENS' TEST — the aldehyde end is oxidised and silver deposited as a mirror:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_2CHO} + 2[\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]^+ + 3\mathrm{OH^-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_2COO^-} + 2\mathrm{Ag}\downarrow + \ldots\)

The molecule responds at both ends, each functional group behaving independently.

rows.stem:
(i) Give a chemical test to distinguish between ethanal acid and ethanoic acid.
(ii) Why is the \(\alpha\)-hydrogens of aldehydes and ketones are acidic in nature ?
(iii) An organic compound 'A' with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_8O_2}\) undergoes acid hydrolysis to form two compounds 'B' and 'C'. Oxidation of 'C' with acidified potassium permanganate also produces 'B'. Sodium salt of 'B' on heating with soda lime gives methane.
(1) Identify 'A', 'B' and 'C'.
(2) Out of 'B' and 'C', which will have higher boiling point ? Give reason.
rows.solution:
(i) [The stem as printed reads "ethanal acid and ethanoic acid"; the marking scheme records this as a MISPRINT and directs full marks for any attempt. The pair intended is ETHANAL and ETHANOIC ACID.]

Add SODIUM HYDROGENCARBONATE solution to each. ETHANOIC ACID gives brisk EFFERVESCENCE of carbon dioxide, being acidic enough to displace it from the salt; ETHANAL gives no reaction at all:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} + \mathrm{NaHCO_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COONa} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{CO_2}\uparrow\)

Tollens' reagent serves in the opposite direction: ethanal gives a silver mirror, ethanoic acid gives nothing, being already at the acid's oxidation level.

(ii) Because the CARBANION left behind is stabilised by RESONANCE with the carbonyl group.

Removing an \(\alpha\) hydrogen leaves a negative charge on the carbon next to the carbonyl, and that charge is immediately delocalised onto the OXYGEN, which is far better able to carry it, being the more electronegative atom:
\(\mathrm{{}^-CH_2{-}CH{=}O} \longleftrightarrow \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}O^-}\)

The resulting ENOLATE is stable enough for a base to remove the hydrogen, which it could never do from an ordinary alkane. This acidity underlies the aldol condensation and \(\alpha\)-halogenation alike.

(iii)(1) Work backwards from the last clue. A sodium salt heated with soda lime loses carbon dioxide and gives the hydrocarbon with ONE CARBON FEWER — so a salt giving METHANE came from a TWO-carbon acid:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\), ethanoic acid

Oxidation of C gives B, and an alcohol oxidises to the acid with the same carbon count:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\), ethanol

Acid hydrolysis of an ESTER gives an acid and an alcohol, and \(\mathrm{C_4H_8O_2}\) fits the ester of these two:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5}\), ethyl ethanoate

(2) ETHANOIC ACID has the higher boiling point — 391 K against ethanol's 351 K.

Both form hydrogen bonds, but the acid forms TWO between each pair of molecules, its carboxyl groups locking together into a DIMER. Ethanol has only one \(\mathrm{O-H}\) per molecule and forms a chain rather than a closed pair, so its association is the weaker of the two.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(a) Why is chemistry of actinoids complicated as compared to lanthanoids ?
(b) Complete the following reaction and justify that it is a disproportionation reaction :
\(3\,\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}} + 4\mathrm{H^{+}} \rightarrow\) ____ + ____ + \(2\,\mathrm{H_2O}\).
(c) The given graph shows the trends in melting points of transition metals :
Explain the reason why Cr has highest melting point and manganese (Mn) a lower melting point.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — sub-part (c) prints a line graph of M.p./\(10^3\)K against Atomic number carrying four labelled series (Ti, Cr, Mn on the 3d curve and Mo, W on the 4d and 5d curves). The two metals the question asks about, Cr and Mn, are both named in the question text, so the row is answerable without reading the plot; the graph is worth showing because the stem refers to it explicitly ('The given graph shows...'). Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
(a) Because actinoid chemistry is complicated by a WIDER RANGE OF OXIDATION STATES and by RADIOACTIVITY.

The lanthanoids are dominated by a single state, \(+3\), with only occasional \(+2\) or \(+4\); their chemistry is correspondingly uniform and predictable. The actinoids show \(+3\) through \(+7\), uranium alone appearing as \(+3\), \(+4\), \(+5\) and \(+6\).

The reason is that the \(5f\), \(6d\) and \(7s\) orbitals lie CLOSE IN ENERGY, so different numbers of electrons can be used for bonding. The \(5f\) orbitals also extend further out than the well-buried \(4f\) orbitals, so they take part in bonding rather than staying inert.

RADIOACTIVITY is the practical complication. Every actinoid is radioactive, and the later members have very short half-lives and are available only in minute quantities, so their chemistry must be studied under conditions that make ordinary measurements difficult.

(b) Completing the equation:
\(3\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}} + 4\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

It is a DISPROPORTIONATION because the SAME element is both oxidised and reduced in the one reaction. Manganese begins at \(+6\) in the manganate ion, and ends in two different states:
TWO of the three manganese atoms rise to \(+7\), in permanganate — OXIDATION.
ONE falls to \(+4\), in manganese dioxide — REDUCTION.

The electrons balance: two atoms lose one each, and one atom gains two.

The green manganate solution turning purple with a brown precipitate is the visible sign, and this is the second stage of the laboratory preparation of potassium permanganate from pyrolusite.

(c) Because CHROMIUM has the most UNPAIRED ELECTRONS available for metallic bonding, and MANGANESE has a stable half-filled subshell that keeps its own from taking part.

The strength of a metallic bond in the transition series depends on how many unpaired d electrons each atom contributes to it. Chromium is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1\) — SIX unpaired electrons, the maximum in the series — so its interatomic bonding is the strongest and its melting point the highest.

Manganese is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^2\). Its \(3d\) subshell is exactly HALF FILLED, an arrangement of unusual stability, so those electrons are held tightly to the atom and are less available for bonding between atoms. Fewer electrons in the metallic bond means a weaker bond and a lower melting point, and manganese falls below both its neighbours.
